segments.t: korTTY can run a terminal session apart from korTTY itself and from the other tabs. You choose how far per connection, per folder of the Connection Manager or for everything in KTPH000Configuration → Global Settings → SecurityKTPH001, and the tab shows what the session actually got.
The session runs in a process of its own.

The process also runs inside the operating system's sandbox: it cannot read or write korTTY's configuration folder KTPH000 (connections, credentials, KTPH001, logs, journals), KTPH002, KTPH003 or the keychains, and it may write only to its working folder, the temporary folder and a folder of its own that is deleted when the session ends.
What each connection type can get in this version:
yes (a local shell is always a process of its own)
yes: KTPH000 runs in the sandbox; the short SSH start of KTPH001 stays in korTTY

A connection that asks for more than its type can get runs with the strongest level it can get, and the connection editor says so under KTPH000Isolation:KTPH001. If your organization demands a level that the connection type cannot get, the session is not opened at all.
The sandbox on each operating system

On macOS korTTY uses KTPH000 with a profile it generates for each session. On Linux it uses bubblewrap (KTPH001), which has to be installed; it needs unprivileged user namespaces, which some containers do not allow. On Windows, and when korTTY runs in Flatpak (itself a sandbox that does not allow another one inside), no sandbox is available yet. Before the first sandboxed session korTTY runs a self-test: a secret file in its configuration folder must be unreadable from inside the sandbox while a harmless command still runs. Only a sandbox that passes counts as available.

In a sandboxed local shell the history file (KTPH000) and KTPH001 point to the session's own folder, so the shell's history does not survive the session, and the variable KTPH002 names the sandbox in use.

KTPH000For one connection:KTPH001 Connection Manager → edit the connection → KTPH002Terminal SettingsKTPH003 tab → KTPH004Session isolationKTPH005 (below KTPH006Terminal behaviorKTPH007) → KTPH008Isolation:KTPH009. KTPH010Use the defaultKTPH011 follows the connection's folder or Settings and names which one applies.

KTPH000For a folder:KTPH001 right-click the folder in the Connection Manager → KTPH002Session IsolationKTPH003 → KTPH004Use the DefaultKTPH005, KTPH006NoneKTPH007, KTPH008Own processKTPH009 or KTPH010Own process + sandboxKTPH011. Folders below inherit the level, and so do the connections in them that set none of their own. The level moves along when the folder is renamed and is removed when the folder is deleted.

KTPH000For everything else:KTPH001 KTPH002Configuration → Global Settings → SecurityKTPH003 → KTPH004Session isolationKTPH005 → KTPH006Default isolation:KTPH007. The section also shows whether this computer has a working sandbox.
A connection from a shared teamwork file can only make isolation stricter than your folder or Settings, never less strict.
Own process inside a verified sandbox; the tooltip names the sandbox (KTPH000 or KTPH001).
A sandbox was asked for but is not active, for example because KTPH000 is missing; the session runs in its own process, and the tooltip says why.

With split panes the shield shows the least isolated pane, except that a missing sandbox always shows the warning sign; the tab's tooltip then counts how many panes run in a sandbox, in their own process, without the requested sandbox and without isolation. Screen readers read the same texts.

KTPH002Strict terminal mode:KTPH003 in the same section drops escape sequences a hostile server could misuse before the terminal sees them: clipboard access (OSC 52), links that are not KTPH000 or KTPH001 links (OSC 8), window titles over 256 characters or with control characters, any OSC sequence over 4 KiB, and device control strings, application program commands, privacy messages and start-of-string sequences. Everything else, including colours, shell-integration marks and the working directory a shell reports, passes unchanged. KTPH004Automatic (on in a sandbox)KTPH005 is the default; KTPH006OnKTPH007 and KTPH008OffKTPH009 set it for the connection. A teamwork connection can switch it on but not off.

An incognito session leaves no trace in korTTY: no terminal log, no session journal, no recording, no entry in KTPH000File → Recently ClosedKTPH001, nothing of its screen in a saved project, and no place in the session that korTTY restores after a restart. Its tab shows a spy. Incognito works with every isolation level, with or without a sandbox.

KTPH000Every session of a connection:KTPH001 tick KTPH002Incognito sessionKTPH003 in the KTPH004Session isolationKTPH005 section of the connection editor. A connection from a shared teamwork file cannot be made incognito.
KTPH000One session:KTPH001 KTPH002File → New Incognito Session…KTPH003 opens Quick Connect; the tab it opens is incognito whatever the connection says.

Incognito concerns what korTTY writes down. The server, a remote shell's own history and anything a program in the session writes are not affected. If your organization enforces a session journal for every session, an incognito session is journaled too, and an organization can forbid incognito sessions altogether.

An enterprise policy can demand a minimum isolation level with KTPH000 and forbid incognito sessions with KTPH001 in KTPH002; see KTPH003Enterprise policyKTPH004. The levels below the minimum are then greyed out everywhere, and a session that cannot get the minimum is refused with a message instead of being opened with less.
